# Testing examples

The definitions of a null hypothesis, a test statistic, a $p$-value, size and power are in [Hypothesis tests](inf-04-hypothesis-tests.qmd). The construction of the most powerful critical region is the [Neyman–Pearson lemma](inf-11-most-powerful-tests.qmd). This page runs the standard tests on data in R and reads the output. The $p$-value R prints is the one defined there: the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true; that calculation is in [Bayesian hypotheses and model comparison](bayes-06-testing.qmd).

## Power by simulation

The power of a test is the probability that it rejects when the null hypothesis is false. For most tests it can be computed by formula, but simulation makes the idea concrete: generate many data sets from a chosen alternative, run the test on each, and count the rejections.

::: {#exm-simulating-the-power-of-a-t-test .example}
## Simulating the power of a t test

A one-sample $t$ test of $H_0:\mu=0$ against $H_1:\mu>0$ is run at level $0.05$ on $n$ observations.

**Question.** What is its power if the data are really $\Normal(1,2^2)$, with $n=5$ and with $n=50$?

**Solution.**

```r
R <- 1e5; n <- 5; mu <- 1; sigma <- 2
pval <- replicate(R, {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  1 - pt(mean(x) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n)), df = n - 1)
})
mean(pval < 0.05)                      # about 0.24
power.t.test(n = 5, delta = 1, sd = 2, sig.level = 0.05,
             type = "one.sample", alternative = "one.sided")$power   # 0.239
```

With five observations the test detects a mean of 1 only 24% of the time. With $n=50$ the power is $0.967$. The power depends on $\mu$ and $\sigma$ only through their ratio $\mu/\sigma$, here $1/2$, together with $n$ and the level. A power calculation of this kind, using a guess at $\sigma$ from a pilot study, is how a sample size is chosen before the data are collected.

:::

![The power of the one-sided one-sample $t$ test at level 0.05 against a true mean of half a standard deviation, as the sample size grows. It passes 0.8 at about $n=27$.](../figures/da-power-by-n.pdf){#fig-da-power-by-n}

## One proportion: exact or approximate

::: {#exm-a-new-sweetener .example}
## A new sweetener

Ten people each taste two yoghurts, one with an old sweetener and one with a new one. Eight prefer the new one.

**Question.** Test whether the new sweetener is preferred, exactly and by the normal approximation.

**Solution.** Let $X\sim\Bin(10,p)$ be the number preferring the new yoghurt, and test $H_0:p=0.5$ against $H_1:p>0.5$. The exact [binomial test](inf-04-hypothesis-tests.qmd#def-binomial-test) has $p$-value $\Pr(X\ge8)=0.0547$:

```r
binom.test(x = 8, n = 10, p = 0.5, alternative = "greater")
# number of successes = 8, number of trials = 10, p-value = 0.05469
```

The normal approximation uses $z=(0.8-0.5)/\sqrt{0.5\times0.5/10}=1.897$, with $p$-value $0.0289$:

```r
prop.test(x = 8, n = 10, p = 0.5, alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)$p.value
# 0.02889
```

The two $p$-values differ by a factor of two, and they fall on opposite sides of $0.05$. Ten observations are too few for the central limit theorem, so the exact test is the one to report. For small samples use `binom.test`.

:::

## Two independent samples

::: {#exm-alices-caffeine-test .example}
## Alice's caffeine test

The heart-rate changes in [Alice's caffeine experiment](da-01-studies-and-data.qmd#exm-alices-caffeine-experiment) were 17, 22, 21, 16, 6, −2, 27, 15, 16, 20 for the caffeinated group and 4, 10, 7, −9, 5, 4, 5, 7, 6, 12 for decaf.

**Question.** Is there evidence that caffeine increases the heart rate?

**Solution.** Model the two groups as independent normal samples with means $\mu_1$ (caffeinated) and $\mu_2$ (decaf), and test $H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2$ against $H_1:\mu_1>\mu_2$.

```r
caf   <- c(17, 22, 21, 16, 6, -2, 27, 15, 16, 20)
decaf <- c(4, 10, 7, -9, 5, 4, 5, 7, 6, 12)
t.test(caf, decaf, alternative = "greater")
# t = 3.3752, df = 15.74, p-value = 0.001966
t.test(caf, decaf, alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value   # 0.001686
```

The difference in means is $10.7$ beats per minute. R's default is the Welch test, with $15.7$ effective degrees of freedom and $p$-value $0.002$; the pooled [two-sample t test](inf-04-hypothesis-tests.qmd#def-two-sample-t-test) gives $p=0.0017$. Either way, a difference this large would be very unlikely without an effect of caffeine. Because the drink was assigned at random, the evidence is evidence that caffeine raises the heart rate, for people like Alice's friends. The two-sided 95% Welch interval for the effect is $(4.0,\ 17.4)$ beats per minute: an effect is clear, its size is not pinned down.

:::

## Paired samples

::: {#exm-two-labs-on-the-same-patients .example}
## Two labs on the same patients

Two labs measure the same quantity on the same 15 patients.

```r
lab1 <- c(22, 18, 28, 26, 13, 8, 21, 26, 27, 29, 25, 24, 22, 28, 15)
lab2 <- c(25, 21, 31, 27, 11, 10, 25, 26, 29, 28, 26, 23, 22, 25, 17)
```

**Question.** Do the labs differ on average?

**Solution.** The two columns are not independent: a patient with a low value gets it from both labs, as patient 6 does with 8 and 10. So analyse the differences $D_i=X_i-Y_i$ as one sample, $D_i\sim\Normal(\delta,\sigma^2)$, and test $H_0:\delta=0$ against $\delta\neq0$:

```r
t.test(lab1, lab2, paired = TRUE)
# t = -1.7618, df = 14, p-value = 0.0999
```

The mean difference is $-0.93$ with standard deviation $2.05$, so $t=-0.93/(2.05/\sqrt{15})=-1.76$ and $p=0.10$. There is weak evidence, at most, that lab 2 reads higher. Ignoring the pairing and running a two-sample test gives $t=-0.42$ and $p=0.68$: the large differences between patients swamp the small, consistent difference between labs. Pairing removes the patient effect.

:::

## Two proportions

For two independent binomial counts, `prop.test` with two counts tests $H_0:p_1=p_2$ with the [two-proportion z test](inf-04-hypothesis-tests.qmd#def-two-proportion-z-test); its printed statistic is the square of $z$, a chi-squared statistic on one degree of freedom. For 40 left-wing viewers out of 70 on one channel against 50 out of 100 on another,

```r
prop.test(c(40, 50), c(70, 100), alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)
# X-squared = 0.8433, df = 1, p-value = 0.1792
```

and $\sqrt{0.8433}=0.918$ is the $z$ statistic. There is no evidence that the first channel's audience is more left-wing.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
State the model and the hypotheses, then let R compute the statistic and the $p$-value. Use the exact binomial test for a small count, pair measurements made on the same unit, and plan the sample size from the power, not after the data are in.
:::

## Exercises

::: {#ex-da-caffeine-cola .exercise}
## Caffeine in a cola

A brand of cola is sampled $n=40$ times. The mean caffeine is 19.57 mg per 6 oz serving and the sample standard deviation is 1.40 mg. The claim under test is that the mean is 19 mg, against the alternative that it is higher.

(a) State the model and the two hypotheses.

(b) Give the test statistic and its null distribution.

(c) Compute the observed statistic, the one-sided p-value, and the decision at level 0.05. Use the fact that the upper tail of $t_{39}$ beyond 2.57 is about 0.007.

[Solution](#sol-da-caffeine-cola)

:::

::: {#ex-da-brexit-poll .exercise}
## A later poll on leaving

A referendum split 51.9% leave and 48.1% remain. A later sample of 500 people has 54% preferring to remain, so 46% preferring to leave. Test whether the leave proportion is still 0.519, against a two-sided alternative.

The standardised statistic is $z=-2.64$, and the two-sided standard-normal tail beyond 2.64 is about 0.0082. Also give an approximate 95% confidence interval for the leave proportion in the later poll.

[Solution](#sol-da-brexit-poll)

:::

::: {#ex-da-steel-rods .exercise}
## Steel rod diameters

Rods should be at least 6 cm in diameter. A sample of 100 rods has mean 6.1 cm and standard deviation 0.1 cm. Assume a normal model.

(a) Estimate the probability that a single rod is thinner than 6 cm.

(b) If the standard deviation stays 0.1 cm, what mean diameter makes 99% of rods at least 6 cm? Use $z_{0.99}=2.326$.

(c) Test $H_0:\mu=6$ against $H_1:\mu>6$. The observed $t$ statistic on 99 degrees of freedom is enormous. What is the conclusion?

[Solution](#sol-da-steel-rods)

:::

::: {#ex-da-shuffle .exercise}
## A shuffling machine

Twenty fresh packs are shuffled. Seventeen have a red card on top. Test whether the top card is still equally likely to be red or black, against the alternative that red is more likely than $1/2$. The one-sided binomial p-value is 0.00174.

[Solution](#sol-da-shuffle)

:::

::: {#ex-da-two-proportions .exercise}
## Two proportions

Independent samples give $\widehat p_X$ and $\widehat p_Y$. The test of $H_0:p_X=p_Y$ against $H_1:p_X>p_Y$ has p-value 0.23. An approximate 99% confidence interval for $p_X-p_Y$ is $(-0.067,\,0.121)$.

(a) State the hypotheses.

(b) What does the p-value say at level 0.05?

(c) Does the interval contain 0?

[Solution](#sol-da-two-proportions)

:::

::: {#ex-da-home-ground .exercise}
## Home-ground wins

Of 25 home games, 20 were wins. Of 75 away games, 55 were wins. Each game is an independent Bernoulli trial, with a probability that depends only on home or away. The two-sample test of equal win probabilities has p-value 0.2526.

State the hypotheses and the conclusion at level 0.05.

[Solution](#sol-da-home-ground)
